A small chunk of data sent across a network; a message is split into many of them.

before.note: HTTP, TCP and TLS are a starting point on this map, with no prerequisite topics. If the three terms below are familiar, you are ready.

stages.name: Basics
body: When your browser loads a page, three layers of rules are at work. HTTP is the language of requests and responses: the client asks for a resource and the server replies with a status and a body. HTTP in turn needs a reliable pipe underneath it, and for most of the web's history that pipe has been TCP.

TCP gives two programs an ordered, reliable stream of bytes, even though the network below it loses and reorders packets. Before any data flows, the two sides set up the connection with a three-way handshake: one side sends a SYN, the other answers with a SYN and an acknowledgment, and the first side acknowledges that [[rfc9293]]. Closing is a separate step, and each side closes its own direction [[rfc9293]].

The handshake costs a round trip before the first request can go out. That is the root of most of what follows: much of the history of HTTP is about paying for fewer round trips and reusing connections once they exist [[mdn-http-evolution]].
HTTP itself began as a one-line protocol with no headers, then grew a version, status codes and headers in HTTP/1.0, and was standardized as HTTP/1.1 with reusable connections [[mdn-http-evolution]].

terms.definition: The request and response language of the web: a method, a resource, headers, and a status in the reply.
A transport protocol that delivers an ordered, reliable stream of bytes between two programs.
The SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK exchange that sets up a TCP connection.
The time a message takes to cross the network; waiting for a reply costs a round trip of it.

stages.name: How it works
body: A new TCP connection does not start at full speed. The sender keeps a congestion window, a limit on how much data may be in flight before an acknowledgment comes back, and the receiver advertises its own window; the smaller of the two governs sending [[rfc5681]]. Slow start begins with a small window and grows it as acknowledgments arrive, probing for how much the network can carry [[rfc5681]].

The starting size matters because most web responses are short. The 2009 standard capped the initial window at a few segments (2, 3 or 4, depending on segment size) [[rfc5681]]. A later experimental document proposed raising the cap to 10 segments, with an upper bound of min(10*MSS, max(2*MSS, 14600)) bytes, and said the increase is optional [[rfc6928]]. A new connection is therefore slow for its first few round trips, which is a strong reason to reuse connections instead of opening new ones.

TLS adds security on top of TCP. Its handshake lets the two sides agree on a version and cryptographic algorithms, optionally authenticate each other, and derive shared keys; after that all application traffic is encrypted with them [[rfc8446]]. In TLS 1.3 the full handshake takes one round trip after the TCP handshake [[rfc8446]].

A client that has talked to a server before can resume. After a handshake the server can hand the client a pre-shared key identity; on a later connection the client offers it and the keys are derived from the earlier connection instead of a full handshake [[rfc8446]]. TLS 1.3 can go further with 0-RTT, sending data in the first flight, but that data has weaker guarantees: it is not forward secret and nothing stops it being replayed between connections [[rfc8446]].
So a first HTTPS request pays for the TCP handshake, then the TLS handshake, then the request itself, all on a connection whose window is still small.

terms.definition: The sender's limit on unacknowledged data in flight, which grows as the network proves it can cope.
The way a new connection grows its window from a small start.

Reusing keys from an earlier connection to skip a full handshake.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: HTTP/1.1 connections are persistent by default: after a response, the same connection carries the next request unless either side sends a close option [[rfc9112]]. Pipelining lets a client send several requests without waiting, but the server must send the responses in the order the requests arrived [[rfc9112]]. One slow response therefore holds up everything behind it on that connection, and browsers worked around it by opening several connections.

HTTP/2 fixes this inside one connection. It splits traffic into streams that are interleaved on the same connection, so many requests proceed in parallel; each side can limit how many streams the other may have open at once [[rfc9113]]. Over TLS it is chosen during the handshake with ALPN, using the identifier h2 [[rfc9113]]. Flow control is credit-based and applies per stream and to the connection as a whole [[rfc9113]].

HTTP/2 still sits on one TCP connection, so a lost packet is retransmitted by TCP and can stall every stream [[mdn-http-evolution]]. QUIC removes that. It runs over UDP, handles loss for each stream separately, and folds the cryptographic and transport handshake into one [[rfc9000]], using TLS 1.3 inside it [[rfc9114]].

HTTP/3 maps HTTP onto QUIC streams. The client's first request goes on stream 0, then 4, 8 and so on, and servers are told to allow at least 100 request streams at once [[rfc9114]]. Client-started streams have even numbers, a rule of how QUIC numbers its streams [[rfc9000]]. HTTP/3 support is announced in the TLS handshake with the ALPN token h3 [[rfc9114]].

terms.definition: A connection kept open to carry more than one request.

A TLS extension in which client and server agree on the application protocol, such as h2 or h3.
A transport built on UDP with streams, loss recovery and TLS 1.3 built in; the base of HTTP/3.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: The practical rule is to pay for a connection once. Clients reuse connections, servers keep them open, and curl does the same when you give it several URLs for one host [[curl-verbose]]. For HTTPS, curl defaults to HTTP/2 when the server supports it, and falls back to HTTP/1.1 when it does not [[curl-http2]].

HTTP/3 cannot be negotiated on an existing TCP connection the way HTTP/2 can, because it uses a different transport and needs its own connection [[curl-http3]]. The official way to bootstrap into it is the Alt-Svc mechanism: a server advertises that it also speaks h3, and the client remembers that for the next request rather than switching mid-request [[curl-http3]]. A fair share of QUIC attempts fail because networks block or throttle UDP, so clients race or fall back to an older version [[curl-http3]].

The trade-offs are concrete. Newer protocols cut waiting but need more of the stack to cooperate. 0-RTT trades safety against replay for speed. Large initial windows trade fairness for faster short transfers. When reading a company post, ask which of these round trips the team removed and what they gave up for it.

You can watch all this yourself. curl in verbose mode prints the connection, the TLS negotiation and the headers [[curl-verbose]], and openssl s_client shows the handshake from the TLS side [[openssl-s-client]].

terms.definition: Sending later requests over a connection that is already open.
A response header by which a server says it is also reachable over another protocol or port, such as h3.
Trying an older protocol when the newer one fails or is blocked.

misconceptions.myth: HTTPS is a separate protocol from HTTP.
misconceptions.truth: It is HTTP carried over a TLS connection; HTTP/2 over TLS is chosen during the TLS handshake with ALPN [[rfc9113]].
It removes it between requests, but all streams share one TCP connection, so a lost packet can still stall them [[mdn-http-evolution]].

misconceptions.myth: HTTP/3 is a new set of HTTP rules.
misconceptions.truth: It keeps the same semantics as earlier versions and changes the transport to QUIC [[mdn-http-evolution]].

misconceptions.myth: TLS 1.3 0-RTT is just a faster handshake.
misconceptions.truth: Its data is not forward secret and can be replayed between connections, so it is weaker than ordinary TLS data [[rfc8446]].

misconceptions.myth: A browser opens a new connection for every request.
misconceptions.truth: HTTP/1.1 connections are persistent by default, and HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are built around reusing one [[rfc9112]].

tryIt.intro: These use curl and openssl, which document the flags used here [[curl-verbose]] [[curl-http2]] [[openssl-s-client]]. The host example.com is the standard example name used in these docs' examples. Run them in a terminal and look for the lines described. Output depends on your tool versions and changes over time, so it is not shown here. A stock macOS curl may not support HTTP/3, so there is no HTTP/3 command.
